content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review:
This work presents an approach for training policies to generate match plans using reinforcement learning. Match plans are used in search engines to retrieve documents for a given user query. One of the challenging features of this problem is that the action space is a mix of discrete and continuous parameters. This work formulates the task as an RL problem, and proposes a number of design decisions for training an effective policy.

This paper presents an interesting application of RL, but overall the technical innovation of the method is fairly modest, and mainly consists of different components that are already commonly used in previous work. The writing also has a fair bit of awkward phrasing and grammatical errors that hurt the clarity of the exposition. For these reasons, I do not think this work meets the bar for ICLR in its current form.

More specific notes:

As someone who is not familiar with search engines, I have some trouble understanding the concept of a match plan from the description provided in the paper. I’m not sure how the rewrite process works. Perhaps adding more details of this, maybe in the appendix, can help readers better understand the task.

The captions for the figures are not very informative.

In Table 2, what is the difference between “prioritized” and “prioritized sample”?

In Figure 3, it is not clear why it is necessary to show the embedding. Most samples seem to show similar performances and it’s not clear if there is any obvious structure. Perhaps this figure can be simply replaced with a history of performances. While Section 4.2 suggests that some clusters with worse or better performance exists, this is not really evident in the plot itself. I’m also not sure what “We guess the reason is that the baseline with hand-crafted rules do not consider the embeddings, thus it is less affected by embeddings.” means. How does the fact that the baseline does not use the embedding affect any structures in the embedding?

The paper provides a fairly thorough review of a lot of different design decisions, but perhaps it is not necessary to go into such excruciating details for all of the different components. Some details such as padding short episodes with zeros are probably not vital for the overall narrative. It might be appropriate to relocate some of these details to the appendix.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 2
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer 2,

Thank you for insightful comments. Based on your concerns, we post more details below for you to better assess our work.

We first provide more details from algorithm side, since our current writing is more from application side.
1. More details from algorithm side
(1) Two types of PARL formulation correspond to two types of action
    - Although we mainly present the experiments in our setting, our proposed method is not only applicable to it. To explain the commonality and difference between it and other benchmarks, we briefly review two slightly different types of PARL formulation.
    - In [Masson et al. (2016)], their formulation Parameterized Action MDP (PAMDP) treats the parameterized action as a hierarchical/sequential manner, which is like to choose an option first and then select a vector of parameters. For example, a robot may use different skills to achieve a different goal, such as moving to a location with its coordinate as the parameters, or grasping an object with its features. The parameters of each skill cannot be shared.
    - However, our setting requires a slightly different formulation, where the parameters are shared across discrete actions. For example, when a robot tries to move an object to a certain location defined by coordinate to maximize its return, the selection of object (action) is not related to the coordinate (parameters). Thus, a policy should treat action and its parameters separately.

(2) A framework also to other applications
- As we review above, many applications can be converted to one of two PARL formulations. We examine different designs and propose a deterministic off-policy agent that can solve them and scale to distributed training setting or larger environments.
- In our method, we argue that P-DQN based method [Xiong et al. (2018)] can only apply to the first formulation. However, our method can effectively solve the second formulation in which our setting belongs to. It can also solve the first formulation, and we provide results on the benchmarks in this formulation.

- [Masson et al. (2016)] Masson, Warwick, Pravesh Ranchod, and George Konidaris. "Reinforcement learning with parameterized actions." Thirtieth AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence. 2016.
- [Xiong et al. (2018)] Jiechao Xiong, Qing Wang, Zhuoran Yang, Peng Sun, Lei Han, Yang Zheng, Haobo Fu, Tong Zhang, Ji Liu, and Han Liu. Parametrized deep q-networks learning: Reinforcement learning with discrete-continuous hybrid action space. arXiv preprint arXiv:1810.06394, 2018.

(3) summary of our contributions
- We formulate the match plan generation as a PARL problem with sharing action-parameters and use a two-headed policy that predicts logits of a categorical distribution for discrete action.
- We propose an exploration strategy on parameter space of policy network for effective exploring on parameterized actions and for target policy smoothing, which solves the inconsistency in exploration with different action space noise on discrete and continuous action.
- To tackle partial observability, we propose a strategy to perturb parameters of RNN-based policy and value networks. We also propose an improved prioritized sampling strategy to increase efficiency.
- We combine those and other improvements such as clipped double Q-learning, n-step return, invertible value function rescaling and form an efficient off-policy agent.
- We evaluate the agent on the match plan generation problem and PARL benchmarks. It outperforms well-designed production match rules and other baselines.

2. More details on application background (see next comment)

3. In Table 2, the difference between “prioritized” and “prioritized sample”
- We missed the explanation of their difference in the experiment section. In the algorithm section, we mention that a modified prioritized experience sampling strategy works slightly better, which we refer as "Prioritized Sample" in this experiment section. The original prioritized experience sampling method [Schaul et al. (2015)] is referred as "Prioritized".
- [Schaul et al. (2015)] Schaul, Tom, et al. "Prioritized experience replay." arXiv preprint arXiv:1511.05952 (2015).

(see next comment)

content.title: Response to Reviewer 2 (cont'd)
content.comment:
2. More details on application background — Match Plan Generation
- In Bing and other web search systems, a key step is the **candidate (documents) generation**, which selects a set of documents from numerous web pages and then ranks and prunes. Bing's candidate generation uses hand-designed **match plans**.
    - A **document** in Bing is represented by several types of descriptions from different sources, called **fields**, and Bing maintains an **inverted index** for each field [Rosset et al. (2018)].
    - The **inverted index** is a specialized data structure that is commonly used in search engines, including Bing. An inverted index provides an inverted mapping from term to documents. Each term has a posting list that contains all the \textit{(document, location)} pairs that the term appears. By combining the posting lists of the terms in a user query, the initial document candidates are generated (\cite{witten1999managing,zobel2006inverted}).
    - A **match plan** is a sequence of **match rule** (named **rewrite**) and **stopping conditions** (named quota). A match rule (rewrite) decides what a document should satisfy to be selected as a candidate for ranking, and the stopping criteria (quota) determines when the index scan using a particular match rule should terminate [Rosset et al. (2018)].
    - In this step, documents are scanned based on a chosen match plan (manually designed or automatically generated) for a search query. The system will then return a set of selected documents. Our goal is to generate a better match plan for each query that balances selected documents' results and execution cost (latency).
    - As for the results' quality, each document will also have a metric (named **Ranking Score**) to evaluate its relevance with the query. Also, the system will return some signals such as consumed resources, and we pick a representative signal (named **Seek Count**) to measure the consumption during the selection of the candidate documents.
    - Intuitively, a match plan is a trade-off between how quickly Bing returns results for a query, and results' quality. For instance, long queries with rare intents may need expensive match plans to consider the body text of the documents and to search deeper into the index to find more candidates [Rosset et al. (2018)]. For a popular navigational query, a shallow scan against a subset of the document fields (such as URL and title) may be sufficient [Rosset et al. (2018)].
- The objective is to maximize the performance of match plans **for each query**. The reward function is intuitively weighted by **Ranking Score** and **Seek Count**. In other words, the goal in match plan generation is to maximize the discounted sum of each step's ranking score and seek count.
    - To make the policy be conditioned on the query, we include the **query embedding** as a part of the state (), which remains constant in one episode. The other part is the intermediate system signals () that partially reflects the system state.
- [Rosset et al. (2018)] gives more comprehensive details on the match plan (match rule) generation.
- [Rosset et al. (2018)] C. Rosset, D. Jose, G. Ghosh, B. Mitra, and S. Tiwary, “Optimizing Query Evaluations Using Reinforcement Learning for Web Search,” presented at the The 41st International ACM SIGIR Conference, New York, New York, USA, 2018, pp. 1193–1196.

4. For the concern of Figure 3
- We present the history of performance of reward (reward curve in some Figures) and the tables of final results in ablation studies.
- The queries are same in evaluating the baseline and the proposed algorithm. Therefore, the corresponding semantic embeddings of those queries are also fixed, and the structure of their embeddings are thus also fixed. In this visualization, we use color to denote the difference between the performance of the proposed algorithm and the production baseline. The color of each point is proportional to the reward of proposed algorithm minus the reward of the production baseline. Thus, the structure of the embedding is not affected by any results. Our goal is to present the relation between queries' information (by their embeddings) and it's relative performance (by the difference of reward values), and we find different values are distributed with certain pattern. This motivates us to further research the relatively poor performance on some clusters of queries, since each query differs dramatically and requires specific attention in usual manual rules.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I did not assess the derivations or theory.
content.review:
This paper presents a parameterized action RL match plan generation method which extends the
plan generation to the general case without any predefined knowledge. Key to address the problem
are normalized softmax values of discrete actions to enable gradients backpropagation, parameter
space noise on parameters of the policy for unifying the exploration direction in both discrete and
continuous spaces, and recurrent deterministic policies with prioritized replay buffer to accelerate
and stabilize the training.

The paper is well written.

Strength: This paper applied RL method on match plan generation. It shows superior performance than manual methods. 

Weakness: Although the experimental results are exciting, the method itself is nothing novel. I do believe this is a good paper but not sure it is the best fit to this conference. 

I am not an expert in this specific area. I'll leave the the decisions to other reviewers and ACs.

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I did not assess the derivations or theory.
content.review:
This paper explores the application of RL to the problem of match plan generation for answering queries in Microsoft Bing.

A potential strength of this paper is to draw attention to a new application of RL, one that potentially has significant social and financial impact. The paper provides some insights into how to cast the problem into the RL framework, in particular the definition of the parameterized action space.

The paper’s weaknesses include:
-	Insufficient detail on some aspects of the problem specification, including a clear explanation of match plan generation, definition of the state space variables, and an explanation of what the transition function might correspond to.
-	The learned policy is only tested on a held-out test set, not in a simulator.  This is not convincing  for RL applications, where the distribution of states changes as a function of the policy, so the estimate of the learned policy will be inaccurate on a policy collected from a different policy (unless correction is applied, e.g. importance sampling, which is not mentioned in the paper).
-	Insights as to how the findings from this new application of RL might inform other applications of RL.  This would be necessary for publication in a venue such as ICLR, where most participants & readers are primarily interested in new methods.
-	The dataset on which training is done is not public.  This is not absolutely necessary, but would certainly increase the value of the paper for the ICLR community.

Additional comments:
-	You seem to use a reward shaping function (bottom of p.6, “Reward design”).  Is this just used for training (as a shaping signal), or also in testing the policy?   It is somewhat concerning that you need to add this explicit signal to modify the policy.
-	The results on the games from Bester et al. (2019) do not necessarily strengthen the paper.  It’s not clear what is “your algorithm” that you test and compare to others, and how the games considered are similar/different than your target application.

    - To make the policy be conditioned on the query, we include the **query embedding** as a part of the state ($s_{emb}\in \mathbb{R}^{100}$), which remains constant in one episode. The other part is the intermediate system signals ($s_{sys}\in \mathbb{R}^{15}$) that partially reflects the system state.
- [Rosset et al. (2018)] gives more comprehensive details on the match plan (match rule) generation.
- [Rosset et al. (2018)] C. Rosset, D. Jose, G. Ghosh, B. Mitra, and S. Tiwary, “Optimizing Query Evaluations Using Reinforcement Learning for Web Search,” presented at the The 41st International ACM SIGIR Conference, New York, New York, USA, 2018, pp. 1193–1196.

2. The concern on "The learned policy is only tested on a held-out test set, not in a simulator"
- We found that some words may cause misunderstanding. The simulator is just a copy of the production Bing environment, and all experiments are conducted on the simulator. The simulator will return several intermediate signals after executing an action, which makes up part of the state. In other words, a state has one part from the simulator system signals and a part of query embedding. For the dataset, we are referring to a set of queries' embeddings, and its distribution is not related to policy.
- Different query indeed has different (semantic) embedding and keeps unchanged during one episode. However, we cannot iterate the continuous embedding space and do not know such high dimensional distribution of queries, thus we use queries collected from Bing engine in a period of time and only remove a few special queries (as we mention in the paper) to keep the queries as uniform as possible.
- We are happy to answer your further concerns on the relation between the distribution of states and the policy, since in general RL setting the distribution of states is indeed a function of policy.
